title: Buddy Petit's luck powder and gamblers' charms
summary: Stories of Petit juggling jobs and winning gigs with a spit-and-chew charm; a gambler on a show.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: But I mean the fella I always played, I didn't find out that John, John, Gundolfa, anyway, Gundolfa. Joe Gundolfa, I asked you about it. They have different bands every Saturday night. Yeah, I should play out on the lake for them all, every Sunday, pretty much when you didn't have to play a parade or something, but down the street show. But see how it goes them days, if you signed a contract with a man there for advertising and another man wants you for a parade, why don't you just call up some of the other musicians and get them to play this and play that? That's all they used to do, see. Buddy Petit could get you with that. He'd get three jobs in one night. The fella going around looking for Buddy with a gun in his pocket. He seemed not to see him, he would kill him, you know. And they walk up on Buddy, Buddy used to food some kind of stuff called luck, you know. And go to spittin', see what he needs you. He said, Buddy, I said, pshw, look at that. I told that fella, I forgot I had that job and I put another fella over there, but I beat on there afterwards. He said, well alright, you come on around there, Buddy, go up there and blow a couple of tunes and leaves and go to another job. Boy, he was a kid up Buddy Petit. What was luck? I don't know except I know what he did. They had a place called the Royal Garden Hall, right there Grab and Ramp Hall. That was his name Royal Garden, on this side of the street. And we wasn't working there. One fella playing up there from over the river, I don't know who he was, so Buddy said, I'm going to get that job. I said, how you going to get it? I'll get it, I'll show you something when I get that job. I went up there, we went to spitting and talking to the man, the man said, hey, you come next Sunday Saturday. That's true. Some kind of stuff, he's putting his mouth and spit his mouth. I said, I don't understand, luck he taught him. He gave him good luck? He must have given him good luck. He waited all the time, time he was ready for a job, he went and got it. Oh, that's true.
You better get some of it. I didn't ever know what it was. I didn't never know what it was. Too bad we never will know. Maybe something, is it that in your book, Barbara, that you read? Luck powder?
Yeah, or something that you chew. It doesn't say anything about chewing it, but they sure sell it over at the Cracker Jacks. Yeah, up there on that pole.

Well, I was on a show last year and a fella had the show. They used to shoot dice. And that man used to lift something in his hand all the time. And he went all the money all the time. Tell you his hand switched. I have to put this pot in my hand, my hand switched, you know. And they put that pot in and boy. He had loaded dice, that would put the food down. Well, it might have been loaded dice too. But I'm telling you, he won all the money every time he shoots dice, he won all the money.
Well, did, did Barthede cook this powder on his hands too? Yeah, he put it all the money. He chewed it and he put it on his hands both.
Yeah, but he had something to put it in his mouth too. Wow. Something like gum. Yeah. But it was black.
Did he tell you where he got it?

He never did tell me. He just tell me I'm going to get a job and say, if you don't believe, come with me now. Sure you're not. But I knew he was using something. I knew he was using something. He didn't walk up and get a job that easy. Yeah. Right. These brass bands, were they your bands?
